title: Grow, Compress, and Perturb: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Pathway to Scalable Quantum Chemistry on Quantum Computers
authors: Hugo D. Nogueira, Siwar Badreddine, Olivier Adjoua, Diata Traore, Guillaume Michel, Jean-Philip Piquemal
abstract: While Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) variants are among leading candidates for electronic structure calculations on quantum computers, gradient-based operator selection limits their scalability. To solve this, we introduce the Hamiltonian-gradient-free VULCAN (Variational Upbuilding, Layered Compression, Adaptive N-body perturbation) layered VQE framework. Our method dynamically generates ansatz operators using Variational Double Bracket Flow (VDBF) equations. Combined with a linearly scaling minimal complete pool, it creates a pool 4-12 times smaller than QEB (Qubit-Excitation-Based) pools. By appending entire layers simultaneously, Hamiltonian gradient measurements are completely eliminated. Circuit depth is managed via a grow-then-compress scheme using efficient state-overlap measurements, and qubit requirements are reduced by projecting the Hamiltonian onto a dominant-determinant subspace. Using high-performance emulation up to 32 logical qubits, we achieve chemical accuracy at just 5-20% of the measurement cost of batched ADAPT-VQE for hydrogen chains, BeH2 and H2O. For the 32-qubit C3H6, where batched ADAPT-VQE does not reach chemical accuracy, a single VULCAN layer combined with a GPU-accelerated stochastic Epstein-Nesbet (ENPT2) correction does. This stochastic ENPT2 post-processing step enables early termination at chemical accuracy.
summary: This paper introduces VULCAN, a novel hybrid quantum-classical algorithm designed to overcome the scalability limits of VQE variants for quantum chemistry. It dynamically builds quantum circuits by growing and compressing operator layers, thereby eliminating costly gradient measurements. This approach achieves chemical accuracy for molecular systems with significantly reduced measurement overhead compared to state-of-the-art adaptive methods.
main_problem: Accurately calculating the ground state energies for strongly correlated many-body systems, which is computationally intractable for classical methods due to Hilbert space size.
main_result: The proposed VULCAN framework achieves chemical accuracy for molecular systems with significantly lower measurement cost (5-20% of ADAPT-VQE) and successfully solves cases where standard adaptive methods fail.
method: A hybrid quantum-classical approach called VULCAN, which uses Variational Double Bracket Flow (VDBF) to generate operators, employs a grow-then-compress scheme to manage circuit depth, and finishes with a stochastic Epstein-Nesbet perturbative correction.
model_or_system: Electronic structure calculations for molecular systems, including hydrogen chains, BeH2, and H2O. The underlying model involves mapping the molecular Hamiltonian onto a qubit representation.
key_observables: Ground state energy, measurement cost (Pauli-term evaluations), CNOT gate count (circuit depth), and the error ($\sigma$) in the ENPT2 correction.
important_parameters: Chemical accuracy ($\sim 1$ kcal/mol), qubit count (up to 32 logical qubits), and the relative scaling of measurement cost compared to ADAPT-VQE.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that the problem can be effectively decomposed into layers that can be added sequentially and compressed, and that classical post-processing (ENPT2) can provide necessary accuracy boosts.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the three primary phases of the VULCAN pipeline: Pool generation, the grow-then-compress loop, and the final perturbative correction.
paper_structure: The paper details the VULCAN framework in three phases: 1) Generating a minimal complete pool using VDBF equations; 2) Iteratively building the ansatz via a grow-then-compress loop; and 3) Applying a stochastic ENPT2 correction for final energy refinement.
why_interesting: The focus on developing resource-efficient quantum algorithms for molecular Hamiltonians directly addresses the core challenge of simulating strongly correlated electron systems on near-term quantum hardware.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Overview of the algorithmic pipeline. Phase 1 generates the operator pool classically: the vDBF flow generator is evaluated as a commutator with the target Hamiltonian and split into individual Pauli strings; operators are added to selected starters among them until a minimal complete pool is obtained, and the remaining vDBF operators are then appended. Phase 2 grows the ansatz one complete layer at a time, optimizing only the parameters of the newly appended layer.
